‘Some of them need a job’: Travis Head hits back at former players after Matthew Hayden's ‘mediocrity’ remark over Australia's recent selection calls

Travis Head hit back at former Australia players after Matthew Hayden's ‘mediocrity’ remark, defending selector and Nic Maddinson's Test recall.

Updated on: Oct 7, 2026, 20:07:10 IST
Written by Probuddha Bhattacharjee
Prefer HTon Google
Share via
Copy link
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 5:24
Instaread

Australian opener Travis Head has hit back at criticism of the current Test side from former players. He accused some of them of effectively “putting the bullet through” players with their commentary. Head spoke about the increasingly hostile discourse around the Australian Test team during a media conference ahead of the first Test between South Africa and Australia.

Although Head did not name any of the former players directly, his comments came at an interesting juncture amid the mounting scrutiny over Australia’s selection calls. The inclusion of Nic Maddinson in the Test side after almost a decade has particularly drawn criticism from a section of former Australian internationals. “I think it’s unfairly judged a fair bit from a group of past players, pretty much that put the bullet through a lot of players, which I think is unfair,” Head said. “But that’s what they’re paid to do. Some of them need a job, so they go after us, and that’s totally fine.”

Matthew Hayden’s criticism of Australian selectors

The criticism intensified after former Australian opener Matthew Hayden questioned Maddinson's inclusion. Hayden called the selection the “greatest pile of mediocrity that we’ve seen in a generation of cricket” and stated that the Australian selectors were showing a lack of respect towards first-class cricket. Maddinson, now 34, was called up as cover after Josh Inglis and Cameron Green suffered injuries. The left-handed batter averages 37.11 in first-class cricket, a figure Hayden used while arguing that players should have stronger domestic numbers before being considered for Test cricket.

Head, though, threw his full support behind the selectors. He also argued that Test cricket often requires players with a firm understanding of their game. “We need mature guys that know what they need to be doing,” he said. “And I think that revolves back to why we’ve been so good over a period of time, and why Australian cricket was so good back then in that era, because you’d bring in the Mike Husseys of the world, who are 30, who are tried and tested and know what they need to do.”

Also Read: What discarded India players can learn from Bhuvneshwar Kumar: Reinvent, adapt and make selectors need you again

Head dismisses debate over his opening role

Travis Head enjoyed considerable success for Australia batting at number five before being tasked with opening the innings in the longest format. Recently, Australian legend Allan Border suggested that opening against the South African attack in the upcoming series could present the sternest examination of Head’s career so far. Border also suggested that the aggressive left-handed batter could be moved back down the order to number five, where he has enjoyed much of his success for Australia in Test cricket.

Head, however, dismissed the discussion around his opening slot. He pointed to his numbers, since moving to the top of the order, to make his case. “I have laughed at a fair bit of it because if a traditional opening batter had pushed out the same sort of numbers in his first 20 innings, I think he’d be pretty safe and not talked about in the way that it has been talked about. It’s a lot of headline stuff,” Head said.

The left-hander also made it clear that the current group of Australian players are mentally equipped to deal with criticism, even when it comes from former greats they grew up respecting. “This group is strong enough to deal with those sorts of things. That’s how it is. It’s unfortunate sometimes to have some of that feedback from a generation of players that we have huge respect for, but that’s the caper,” Head said.

Kamal Haasan writes to Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar urging him to meet Opposition MPs: Integrity of our electoral process is under strain

Kamal Haasan shared the letter, in which he added that the public confidence in the independence of the Election Commission seems to be weakening.

Published on: Oct 7, 2026, 21:39:24 IST
By Santanu Das
Prefer HTon Google
Share via
Copy link

Opposition MPs of the INDIA bloc held a sit-in protest at Ashoka Road on Wednesday to raise the issue of 'vote chori' and seek the ouster of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, a day after their eight-hour dharna to press for a meeting with election commissioners. Now actor and member of Parliament, Kamal Haasan, has written a letter to Gyanesh Kumar and urged him to meet the Opposition MPs and address the concerns that are being raised.

Kamal Haasan's letter

In the letter posted on X, Kamal wrote with the subject line: ‘An Appeal for restoring public trust in the Election Commission of India.’

He began, “The right to vote is among the most fundamental expressions of our democracy. The Election Commission of India, as the constitutional institution entrusted with safeguarding that right, occupies a uniquely sacred position in our Republic.”

Deep Dive

Powered ByAsk HT

“Over recent years, however, a series of developments have contributed to a growing perception among the citizens of India, that the integrity of our electoral process is under strain. Concerns have been raised over the rushed, and in some instances, erroneous implementation of Special Intensive Revision and the resulting apprehensions of disenfranchisement… The process of protecting the electoral role must never a barrier to exercising the right to vote,” he added.

How David Warner, Steve Smith and Cameron Bancroft’s evil tampering plot was caught on camera: ‘It was an absolute fluke’

From the horse’s mouth. Alvin Naicker, who was in charge of the live broadcast of the Third Test in Newlands, reveals it all.

Updated on: Oct 8, 2026, 08:13:03 IST
Written by Prateek Srivastava
Prefer HTon Google
Share via
Copy link

South Africa and Australia kick off their three-Test series at Kingsmead on Friday. This is Australia’s first Test visit to South Africa since the infamous, sandpapergate series in 2018. To jog one’s memory, what happened at Newlands was this: Cameron Bancroft, in complicity with captain Steve Smith and David Warner, used sandpaper secretly to tamper with the ball to be able to assist pacers with reverse swing.

With the first Test set to begin tomorrow, the sandpapergate is being discussed at length all over the global media. Alvin Naicker, the man in charge that day of SuperSport’s live coverage, reveals to BBC Sport, that catching Bancroft in the act was accidental. His team was doing its regular work, just when it was discovered, to their utter shock, what was happening on the field of play.

Also Read: Is making Vaibhav Sooryavanshi wait the right call? India wrestle with a selection dilemma around their 15-year-old batting prodigy

"The way the Australians were caught was an absolute fluke,” Naicker said. "No one mentioned anything to me. The first Test in Durban spiralled out of control in terms of behaviour, then in Port Elizabeth for the second Test, there were still some fireworks going on. We still didn't understand.

"The ball went to the wicketkeeper, then to Bancroft, and he was shining the ball. First, it was on his pants, then the next ball, the cameraman happened to stay on Bancroft because he was not shining the ball on his pants, but he was rubbing the ball on his palm.
